opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The assertion is true because a uniform ring has complete symmetry about its centre. Equal mass elements on opposite sides of the centre balance their position contributions. The reason is false because the material of a ring is not concentrated at the centre; it is distributed around the circumference. The centre of mass lies at the centre because of symmetry, not because material is physically present there. This distinction prevents the mistaken idea that centre of mass must always be an occupied point.

question: A uniform semicircular wire has less symmetry than a complete circular ring. Its centre of mass is expected to lie
opt_a: at the centre of the original full circle
opt_b: at either end of the semicircular wire
opt_c: on the symmetry axis of the semicircle
opt_d: at every point of the circular arc
explanation: A semicircular wire still has one line of symmetry passing through the midpoint of the arc and the centre of the original circle. Mass elements on the left and right sides of this symmetry line balance each other. Therefore, the centre of mass must lie on this symmetry axis. However, the upper and lower parts are not symmetrically distributed like a complete ring, so it need not lie at the centre of the original circle. Symmetry can restrict the possible line of location even when it does not give the exact point immediately.

question: For a composite body made of simple parts, the centre of mass can often be found by
opt_a: using only the outermost dimensions of the body
opt_b: treating each part as concentrated at its centre of mass
opt_c: placing it at the geometrical centre in every case
opt_d: ignoring the masses of larger parts of the composite body
explanation: A composite body can be divided into simpler parts whose individual centres of mass are known. For centre-of-mass calculation, each part may be replaced by a point mass located at its own centre of mass. The mass of that part is then used in the weighted-average formula. This method works because centre of mass depends on total mass and mass-weighted position, not on the detailed shape after each part's centre of mass is known. The geometrical centre is safe only for uniform symmetric bodies, not for every composite body.

question: A uniform rod of length \(3L\) is made by joining two uniform rods along the same line: one has length \(L\) and mass \(m\), and the other has length \(2L\) and mass \(2m\). The rods are joined end to end, with the shorter rod on the left. Measured from the left end, the centre of mass is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Parts of the body:} \) The shorter rod has mass \(m\) and length \(L\); the longer rod has mass \(2m\) and length \(2L\).
\( \textbf{Choose origin:} \) Take the left end of the shorter rod as \(x=0\).
\( \textbf{Centre of shorter rod:} \)
\[
x_1=\frac{L}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Centre of longer rod:} \) The longer rod extends from \(x=L\) to \(x=3L\), so its centre is
\[
x_2=2L
\]
\( \textbf{Composite centre-of-mass formula:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)+2m(2L)}{m+2m}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplify numerator:} \)
\[
\frac{mL}{2}+4mL=\frac{9mL}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Divide by total mass:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\frac{9mL}{2}}{3m}=\frac{3L}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Option check:} \) The value \(\frac{3L}{2}\) lies between \(L\) and \(2L\), closer to the longer rod because that rod has the greater mass.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is at \(\frac{3L}{2}\) from the left end.

question: A uniform rod of length \(2L\) has its left half made of material with mass \(m\) and its right half made of material with mass \(3m\). The centre of mass from the left end is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Divide the rod:} \) Treat the left half and right half as two uniform parts.
\( \textbf{Masses:} \) Left half has mass \(m\), and right half has mass \(3m\).
\( \textbf{Centres of the parts:} \) The left half extends from \(0\) to \(L\), so \(x_1=\frac{L}{2}\).
\( \textbf{Centre of right half:} \) The right half extends from \(L\) to \(2L\), so \(x_2=\frac{3L}{2}\).
\( \textbf{Composite relation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m\left(\frac{L}{2}\right)+3m\left(\frac{3L}{2}\right)}{m+3m}
\]
\( \textbf{Numerator:} \)
\[
\frac{mL}{2}+\frac{9mL}{2}=5mL
\]
\( \textbf{Denominator:} \)
\[
m+3m=4m
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{5mL}{4m}=\frac{5L}{4}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is \(\frac{5L}{4}\) from the left end, shifted toward the heavier right half.

question: In the negative-mass method for a lamina with a hole, the removed part is treated as
opt_a: zero mass placed only at the chosen origin
opt_b: a force acting at the edge of the hole
opt_c: a positive mass at the centre of mass of the removed part
opt_d: a negative mass at the removed part's centre of mass
explanation: A body with a hole can be treated as a complete body plus a removed part having negative mass. The negative mass is placed at the centre of mass of the removed portion. This method keeps the weighted-average formula usable without separately describing the complicated remaining shape. The total mass used in the denominator is the mass of the complete body minus the removed mass. The sign is only a calculation device for removed material, not a claim that real negative mass exists in the lamina.

question: A uniform square lamina of side \(2a\) has a small square of side \(a\) removed from one corner. To set up the centre-of-mass calculation using the subtraction method, the correct idea is to use
opt_a: the geometrical centre of the original square without any correction
opt_b: only the outer boundary of the remaining shape
opt_c: the full square as positive mass and the removed square as negative mass
opt_d: the removed square as positive mass and the full square as negative mass
explanation: In the subtraction method, the original complete lamina is first treated as a positive mass located at its own centre of mass. The removed portion is then treated as a negative mass located at the centre of mass of that removed portion. The centre of mass of the remaining body is found by applying the usual weighted-average formula with these signed masses. This works because removing material reduces the mass contribution from that region. The original geometrical centre alone is no longer enough because the missing corner breaks the symmetry.

question: A composite body is made by joining two point-replaceable parts. Part P has mass \(2M\) and its own centre at \(x=0\). Part Q has mass \(M\) and its own centre at \(x=6a\). The centre of mass of the composite body is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Composite-body model:} \) Treat each part as a point mass at its own centre of mass.
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Part P has mass \(2M\) at \(x=0\), and part Q has mass \(M\) at \(x=6a\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) \(X_{\text{CM}}\) of the two-part composite body.
\( \textbf{Relation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_Px_P+m_Qx_Q}{m_P+m_Q}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(2M)(0)+(M)(6a)}{2M+M}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{6Ma}{3M}
\]
\( \textbf{Cancel the common mass factor:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=2a
\]
\( \textbf{Physical check:} \) The result is closer to the heavier part P at \(x=0\), so \(2a\) is reasonable.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is at \(x=2a\).

question: A uniform square lamina of side \(2a\) has a square of side \(a\) removed from its upper-right corner. Take the centre of the original square as origin, with axes parallel to its sides. The centre of the removed square is at \(\left(\frac{a}{2},\frac{a}{2}\right)\). If the full square has mass \(4m\), the centre of mass of the remaining lamina is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Complete lamina:} \) The full square has mass \(4m\) and centre of mass at \((0,0)\).
\( \textbf{Removed part:} \) The removed square has side \(a\), so its mass is \(m\), and it is treated as negative mass at \(\left(\frac{a}{2},\frac{a}{2}\right)\).
\( \textbf{Remaining mass:} \)
\[
M_{\text{rem}}=4m-m=3m
\]
\( \textbf{x-coordinate:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(4m)(0)-m\left(\frac{a}{2}\right)}{3m}
\]
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=-\frac{a}{6}
\]
\( \textbf{y-coordinate:} \)
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(4m)(0)-m\left(\frac{a}{2}\right)}{3m}
\]
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=-\frac{a}{6}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction check:} \) Mass is removed from the upper-right corner, so the remaining centre of mass shifts toward the lower-left side.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is \(\left(-\frac{a}{6},-\frac{a}{6}\right)\).

question: A uniform disc has a small circular hole cut out away from its centre. For locating the centre of mass of the remaining lamina, the most suitable modelling step is to
opt_a: ignore the removed part because it contains no material now
opt_b: keep the centre of mass at the original disc centre in every off-centre case
opt_c: treat the hole as a negative mass placed at the hole's centre
opt_d: place the whole remaining mass at the rim of the large disc
explanation: A hole is handled by treating the removed portion as negative mass in the centre-of-mass formula. For a circular hole, the removed part's mass may be placed at the centre of that small circle because the removed circular part is itself uniform and symmetric. The full disc is treated as positive mass at its original centre. The remaining lamina's centre of mass comes from the weighted average of the positive full disc and the negative removed disc. If the hole is off-centre, the original symmetry is broken, so the centre of mass generally shifts away from the hole.

question: A composite body is formed by joining two uniform rods at right angles. Rod P of mass \(m\) and length \(2a\) lies along the \(x\)-axis from \(x=0\) to \(x=2a\). Rod Q of mass \(2m\) and length \(2a\) lies along the \(y\)-axis from \(y=0\) to \(y=2a\). The centre of mass of the composite body is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Rod P:} \) It lies from \(x=0\) to \(x=2a\), so its centre is at \((a,0)\), and its mass is \(m\).
\( \textbf{Rod Q:} \) It lies from \(y=0\) to \(y=2a\), so its centre is at \((0,a)\), and its mass is \(2m\).
\( \textbf{Total mass:} \)
\[
M=m+2m=3m
\]
\( \textbf{x-coordinate:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m(a)+2m(0)}{3m}
\]
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{a}{3}
\]
\( \textbf{y-coordinate:} \)
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m(0)+2m(a)}{3m}
\]
\[
Y_{\text{CM}}=\frac{2a}{3}
\]
\( \textbf{Mass-distribution check:} \) The heavier vertical rod pulls the centre of mass closer to the \(y\)-axis and upward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass is \(\left(\frac{a}{3},\frac{2a}{3}\right)\).

question: A uniform lamina is made by joining a square plate of mass \(4m\) with a smaller square plate of mass \(m\) along one side. Their individual centres lie on the same horizontal line and are separated by \(3a\). Measured from the centre of the larger square toward the smaller square, the centre of mass is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Composite-body idea:} \) Replace each square plate by a point mass at its own centre of mass.
\( \textbf{Choose origin:} \) Take the centre of the larger square as \(x=0\).
\( \textbf{Mass-position data:} \) Larger square: mass \(4m\), position \(0\). Smaller square: mass \(m\), position \(3a\).
\( \textbf{Required coordinate:} \) \(X_{\text{CM}}\) measured from the larger square's centre.
\( \textbf{Formula:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1x_1+m_2x_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(4m)(0)+m(3a)}{4m+m}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{3ma}{5m}
\]
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{3a}{5}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass lies \(\frac{3a}{5}\) from the larger square's centre toward the smaller square.

question:
Study the table and choose the row that gives a suitable composite-body replacement.
RowBody partReplacement for centre-of-mass calculation
PUniform rod segmentPoint mass at its midpoint
QUniform circular discPoint mass at any point on the rim
RRemoved uniform partPositive mass at the removed part's centre
SUniform rectangular platePoint mass at one corner
explanation: A uniform rod segment has its centre of mass at its midpoint, so it can be replaced by a point mass at that point for a composite-body calculation. A uniform disc is replaced by a point mass at its centre, not at an arbitrary point on the rim. A removed part is treated as negative mass, not positive mass, when using the subtraction method. A uniform rectangular plate is replaced by a point mass at the intersection of its diagonals, not at a corner. The replacement point must be the centre of mass of that individual part.

question: A body is made by removing a small mass \(m\) at \(x=4a\) from a larger uniform body of mass \(5m\) whose centre is at \(x=0\). The centre of mass of the remaining body is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Full body:} \) Treat the larger body as mass \(5m\) at \(x=0\).
\( \textbf{Removed part:} \) Treat the removed mass as negative mass \(-m\) at \(x=4a\).
\( \textbf{Remaining mass:} \)
\[
M_{\text{rem}}=5m-m=4m
\]
\( \textbf{Use signed-mass average:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(5m)(0)+(-m)(4a)}{4m}
\]
\( \textbf{Numerator:} \)
\[
(5m)(0)-4ma=-4ma
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{-4ma}{4m}=-a
\]
\( \textbf{Direction check:} \) Removing mass from the positive side shifts the remaining centre of mass toward the negative side.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass of the remaining body is at \(x=-a\).

question:
Consider the following statements about composite-body centre-of-mass calculations.
I. Each simple part may be replaced by its mass placed at its own centre of mass.
II. The coordinate origin can be chosen for convenience, but all part coordinates must then use the same origin.
III. Removed material is treated as positive mass at the centre of the removed part.
explanation: Statement I is true because the detailed shape of a simple part can be replaced by its total mass at its own centre of mass. Statement II is true because the coordinate origin is a calculation choice, but consistency is necessary once it is chosen. Statement III is false in the subtraction method because removed material is treated as negative mass. Using positive mass for the removed part would shift the centre of mass toward the missing region instead of away from it. The sign of the removed mass is the key difference between adding parts and cutting parts out.

question: A uniform rod of length \(4a\) has a segment of length \(a\) cut off from its right end. If the original rod's left end is taken as \(x=0\), the centre of mass of the remaining rod is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Remaining part:} \) Cutting off the rightmost length \(a\) leaves a uniform rod from \(x=0\) to \(x=3a\).
\( \textbf{Direct symmetry method:} \) The remaining rod is uniform and straight.
\( \textbf{Centre of a uniform rod:} \) Its centre of mass lies at the midpoint of its remaining length.
\( \textbf{Remaining length:} \)
\[
L_{\text{rem}}=3a
\]
\( \textbf{Midpoint from the left end:} \)
\[
X_{\text{CM}}=\frac{3a}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Subtraction interpretation:} \) The removed part was on the right side, so the centre of mass moves left from the original midpoint \(2a\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass of the remaining rod is at \(\frac{3a}{2}\).

question: The velocity of the centre of mass of a system of particles is given by
explanation: The velocity of the centre of mass is the mass-weighted average of the velocities of all particles in the system. The term \(m_i\vec{v}_i\) is the momentum contribution of the \(i^{\text{th}}\) particle. Dividing the sum of these terms by the total mass \(M\) gives a velocity. The formula is vectorial, so directions of the individual velocities matter. It is not a simple average unless all particles have equal masses.

question: Two particles of masses \(2\,\text{kg}\) and \(3\,\text{kg}\) move along the \(x\)-axis with velocities \(4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(-1\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), respectively. The velocity of the centre of mass is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(v_1=4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(m_2=3\,\text{kg}\), and \(v_2=-1\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) \(V_{\text{CM}}\) along the \(x\)-axis.
\( \textbf{Useful relation:} \)
\[
V_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1v_1+m_2v_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Why signs matter:} \) The velocities are along the same axis, and the negative sign shows motion opposite to the positive direction.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
V_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(2)(4)+(3)(-1)}{2+3}\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Numerator:} \)
\[
8-3=5
\]
\( \textbf{Denominator:} \)
\[
2+3=5
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
V_{\text{CM}}=\frac{5}{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}=1\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass moves with velocity \(1\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) in the positive \(x\)-direction.

question: A two-particle system has equal masses. One particle moves east with speed \(v\), and the other moves west with the same speed \(v\). The velocity of the centre of mass is
explanation: Equal masses moving with equal speeds in opposite directions have equal and opposite momentum contributions. The velocity of the centre of mass depends on the vector sum \(m\vec{v}+m(-\vec{v})\). This sum is zero, so \(\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}=\vec{0}\). The particles themselves are moving, but the representative point of the whole system remains at rest if no other motion is involved. This shows that internal relative motion and centre-of-mass motion are different descriptions.

question: The acceleration of the centre of mass is expressed as
explanation: The acceleration of the centre of mass follows the same weighted-average structure as position and velocity. Each particle acceleration is weighted by the corresponding mass. The denominator is the total mass \(M\), so the result has the unit of acceleration, \(\text{m s}^{-2}\). This relation is especially useful because it connects naturally with the net external force on a system. The acceleration of the centre of mass is controlled by the system-level balance, not by simply choosing the largest individual acceleration.

question: A system consists of two particles of masses \(m\) and \(3m\). Their accelerations along a line are \(4a\) and \(-2a\), respectively. The acceleration of the centre of mass is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) The masses are \(m\) and \(3m\).
\( \textbf{Accelerations:} \) \(a_1=4a\) and \(a_2=-2a\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) \(A_{\text{CM}}\) along the given line.
\( \textbf{Formula:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1a_1+m_2a_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m(4a)+3m(-2a)}{m+3m}
\]
\( \textbf{Numerator:} \)
\[
4ma-6ma=-2ma
\]
\( \textbf{Denominator:} \)
\[
m+3m=4m
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{-2ma}{4m}=-\frac{a}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Sign meaning:} \) The heavier particle has acceleration in the negative direction, so it dominates the weighted average.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The acceleration of the centre of mass is \(-\frac{a}{2}\).

question: A firecracker initially at rest explodes into two fragments on a smooth horizontal surface. During the short explosion, horizontal external force is negligible. The centre of mass
opt_a: starts moving in the direction of the heavier fragment
opt_b: starts moving in the direction of the lighter fragment
explanation: The explosion produces large internal forces between the fragments. These internal forces can change the velocities of the individual fragments, sending them in different directions. However, if the net external horizontal force is negligible, the motion of the centre of mass is not changed by those internal forces. Since the firecracker was initially at rest, the centre of mass remains at rest during and after the explosion in the horizontal description. The fragments may separate rapidly even though the centre-of-mass motion is unchanged.

question: A system has total mass \(M\). If the net external force on it is \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}\), the centre-of-mass acceleration is connected by
explanation: The centre of mass of a system moves as if the total external force acts on the total mass of the system. The relation is \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=M\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\). Internal forces may redistribute motion among the particles, but they do not determine the acceleration of the centre of mass when they cancel in action-reaction pairs. The equation is a system-level form of Newton's second law. It uses external force, not the sum of internal pushes and pulls.

question: A \(10\,\text{kg}\) system has a net external force of \(30\,\text{N}\) acting toward the positive \(x\)-direction. The acceleration of its centre of mass is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Total mass \(M=10\,\text{kg}\), and net external force \(F_{\text{ext}}=30\,\text{N}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Acceleration of the centre of mass \(A_{\text{CM}}\).
\( \textbf{System-level Newton's second law:} \)
\[
F_{\text{ext}}=MA_{\text{CM}}
\]
\( \textbf{Rearrange for acceleration:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{F_{\text{ext}}}{M}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{30\,\text{N}}{10\,\text{kg}}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit conversion check:} \) Since \(1\,\text{N}=1\,\text{kg m s}^{-2}\), \(\frac{\text{N}}{\text{kg}}=\text{m s}^{-2}\).
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=3\,\text{m s}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction:} \) The acceleration is in the positive \(x\)-direction because the net external force is in that direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass accelerates at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) toward positive \(x\).

question: A system of two blocks is pulled horizontally by an external force of \(18\,\text{N}\). The blocks have masses \(2\,\text{kg}\) and \(4\,\text{kg}\). Ignoring friction, the acceleration of the centre of mass is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(F_{\text{ext}}=18\,\text{N}\), \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), and \(m_2=4\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Total mass:} \)
\[
M=m_1+m_2=2\,\text{kg}+4\,\text{kg}=6\,\text{kg}
\]
\( \textbf{System-level relation:} \)
\[
F_{\text{ext}}=MA_{\text{CM}}
\]
\( \textbf{Why this applies:} \) The acceleration of the centre of mass is decided by the net external force on the chosen system.
\( \textbf{Rearrange:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{F_{\text{ext}}}{M}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{18\,\text{N}}{6\,\text{kg}}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit check:} \)
\[
\frac{\text{N}}{\text{kg}}=\text{m s}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=3\,\text{m s}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass accelerates at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) in the direction of the external force.

question: Two people standing on smooth ice push each other apart. If the system consists of both people and horizontal external force is negligible, the centre of mass of the two-person system
explanation: The push between the two people is an internal interaction when both people are included in the same system. Internal forces can change the motion of each person separately, but they cannot change the motion of the centre of mass of the whole system. With negligible horizontal external force, \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=0\), so \(\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}=0\). Therefore, the centre of mass continues with constant velocity. If it was initially at rest, it remains at rest while the two people move apart.

question:
Consider the following statements about the motion of the centre of mass.
I. Internal forces can change the velocities of particles inside the system.
II. Internal forces alone can change \(\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\) of the system.
III. A non-zero net external force is needed to change \(\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\).
explanation: Statement I is true because particles inside a system can exert forces on one another and change one another's individual velocities. Statement II is false for ordinary internal action-reaction pairs because internal forces cancel in the system-level force balance. Statement III is true because changing \(\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\) requires non-zero \(\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\), and \(M\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}=\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}\). Internal motion and centre-of-mass motion are not the same thing. The centre of mass responds to the net external force on the chosen system.

question: A trolley of mass \(5\,\text{kg}\) moving at \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) is acted on by a constant external force of \(10\,\text{N}\) in the direction of motion for \(3\,\text{s}\). Treating the trolley as a system, its centre-of-mass speed after \(3\,\text{s}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(M=5\,\text{kg}\), initial speed \(u_{\text{CM}}=2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), force \(F_{\text{ext}}=10\,\text{N}\), and time \(t=3\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Find centre-of-mass acceleration:} \)
\[
F_{\text{ext}}=MA_{\text{CM}}
\]
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{F_{\text{ext}}}{M}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{10\,\text{N}}{5\,\text{kg}}=2\,\text{m s}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Kinematic relation:} \)
\[
v_{\text{CM}}=u_{\text{CM}}+A_{\text{CM}}t
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v_{\text{CM}}=2+(2)(3)
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
v_{\text{CM}}=8\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction check:} \) The force acts along the motion, so the speed increases.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre-of-mass speed becomes \(8\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question:
Study the table and identify the row with the correct system-level conclusion.
RowCondition on chosen systemConclusion for centre of mass
P\(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=0\)\(\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}=0\)
QInternal forces are large\(\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\) must be large
RParticles move relative to each other\(\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\) must be zero
SMasses are unequalCentre of mass cannot be defined
explanation: Row P is correct because \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=M\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\), so zero net external force gives zero centre-of-mass acceleration. Row Q is not reliable because large internal forces can change internal motion without changing the system's centre-of-mass acceleration. Row R is false because particles may move relative to one another while the centre of mass moves uniformly or remains at rest depending on total momentum. Row S is false because unequal masses are handled naturally by mass-weighted averages. The centre-of-mass description is a system-level description, not a statement that all particles move together.

question:
Use the graph description below.
For a system of constant total mass \(M\), a graph of \(V_{\text{CM}}\) versus \(t\) is a straight line with positive slope.
What does the slope of this graph represent?
explanation: In a velocity-time graph, the slope gives acceleration. Since the plotted velocity is \(V_{\text{CM}}\), the slope represents \(A_{\text{CM}}\). If the slope is positive, the centre-of-mass velocity is increasing in the chosen positive direction. For a constant mass system, the net external force is then related by \(F_{\text{ext}}=MA_{\text{CM}}\). The graph does not directly give internal force, because internal forces are not what controls the acceleration of the centre of mass.

question: A \(12\,\text{kg}\) system has a centre-of-mass acceleration of \(0.5\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) toward the west. The net external force on the system is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Total mass \(M=12\,\text{kg}\), and centre-of-mass acceleration \(A_{\text{CM}}=0.5\,\text{m s}^{-2}\) toward west.
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Net external force on the system.
\( \textbf{System relation:} \)
\[
\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=M\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}
\]
\( \textbf{Magnitude calculation:} \)
\[
F_{\text{ext}}=(12)(0.5)\,\text{N}
\]
\[
F_{\text{ext}}=6\,\text{N}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction:} \) Since mass is positive, \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}\) has the same direction as \(\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\).
\( \textbf{Unit check:} \)
\[
\text{kg m s}^{-2}=\text{N}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The net external force is \(6\,\text{N}\) toward west.

question: A system is made of two particles. One particle has mass \(2m\) and acceleration \(3a\) to the right. The other has mass \(m\) and acceleration \(6a\) to the left. Taking right as positive, \(A_{\text{CM}}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Sign convention:} \) Take right as positive, so the accelerations are \(+3a\) and \(-6a\).
\( \textbf{Masses:} \) \(m_1=2m\) and \(m_2=m\).
\( \textbf{Formula:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{m_1a_1+m_2a_2}{m_1+m_2}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{(2m)(3a)+m(-6a)}{2m+m}
\]
\( \textbf{Numerator:} \)
\[
6ma-6ma=0
\]
\( \textbf{Denominator:} \)
\[
3m
\]
\( \textbf{Result:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=0
\]
\( \textbf{Physical meaning:} \) The mass-weighted accelerations cancel, so the centre of mass has no acceleration along the chosen line.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(A_{\text{CM}}=0\).

question: The total linear momentum of a system of particles is written as
explanation: The total linear momentum of a system is the vector sum of the momenta of all particles in that system. If the \(i^{\text{th}}\) particle has momentum \(\vec{p}_i=m_i\vec{v}_i\), then \(\vec{P}=\sum \vec{p}_i\). Momentum is a vector, so opposite directions can cancel partly or completely. The expression \(\sum m_i\vec{r}_i\) belongs to centre-of-mass position, not momentum. Total momentum measures the system's overall translational motion.

question: The relation between total momentum and centre-of-mass velocity is
explanation: The velocity of the centre of mass is \(\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum m_i\vec{v}_i\). The numerator \(\sum m_i\vec{v}_i\) is exactly the total momentum \(\vec{P}\) of the system. Multiplying both sides by \(M\) gives \(\vec{P}=M\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\). This relation shows why the centre of mass is useful for translational motion of a many-particle system. It connects a system-level velocity with the total vector momentum.

question: Two particles of masses \(1\,\text{kg}\) and \(2\,\text{kg}\) move along the same line with velocities \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(-3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), respectively. The total momentum of the system is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(m_1=1\,\text{kg}\), \(v_1=6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(m_2=2\,\text{kg}\), and \(v_2=-3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Total momentum \(P\) along the line.
\( \textbf{Momentum sum:} \)
\[
P=m_1v_1+m_2v_2
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution with signs:} \)
\[
P=(1)(6)+(2)(-3)
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
P=6-6=0
\]
\( \textbf{Unit:} \) Linear momentum is measured in \(\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Centre-of-mass link:} \) Since \(\vec{P}=M\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\), zero total momentum means the centre of mass is at rest along this line.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The total momentum is \(0\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

question: A system has total momentum \(\vec{P}=20\,\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) and total mass \(5\,\text{kg}\). Its centre-of-mass velocity is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(\vec{P}=20\,\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\), and \(M=5\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) \(\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\).
\( \textbf{Relation:} \)
\[
\vec{P}=M\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}
\]
\( \textbf{Rearrange:} \)
\[
\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}=\frac{\vec{P}}{M}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}=\frac{20\,\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}}{5\,\text{kg}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}=4\,\hat{i}\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction check:} \) The centre-of-mass velocity has the same direction as the total momentum.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}=4\,\hat{i}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: A system has non-zero total momentum. This necessarily means that
opt_b: the net external force must be zero
opt_c: its centre of mass has non-zero velocity
opt_d: every particle must move in the same direction
explanation: The total momentum of a system is related to centre-of-mass velocity by \(\vec{P}=M\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\). Since the total mass \(M\) is positive, non-zero \(\vec{P}\) implies non-zero \(\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\). This does not require all particles to move in the same direction; their vector momenta may partly cancel and still leave a non-zero resultant. Internal forces may exist while total momentum is being considered. Net external force decides how \(\vec{P}\) changes with time, not whether \(\vec{P}\) is non-zero at an instant.

question:
Study the table and identify the row with the incorrect statement about total momentum.
RowStatement
P\(\vec{P}\) is the vector sum of all particle momenta.
Q\(\vec{P}=M\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\).
ROpposite momenta can cancel in the total momentum.
STotal momentum is found by adding only the magnitudes of individual momenta.
explanation: Momentum is a vector quantity, so direction must be included when momenta are added. Row P is correct because total momentum is \(\vec{P}=\sum \vec{p}_i\). Row Q is correct because the total momentum equals total mass times centre-of-mass velocity. Row R is also correct because equal and opposite momenta can cancel. Row S is incorrect because adding only magnitudes ignores direction and can give a wrong total momentum.

question: A graph of total momentum \(P\) versus centre-of-mass velocity \(V_{\text{CM}}\) for a fixed system is a straight line through the origin. The slope of the graph represents
opt_d: displacement of the centre of mass
explanation: The relation between total momentum and centre-of-mass velocity is \(P=MV_{\text{CM}}\) for one-dimensional motion. This has the graph form \(Y=(\text{slope})X\), where \(Y=P\) and \(X=V_{\text{CM}}\). Therefore, the slope is \(M\). The graph passes through the origin because zero centre-of-mass velocity gives zero total momentum. The slope tells how much momentum the system has for each unit of centre-of-mass velocity.

question: A body of mass \(3\,\text{kg}\) moving at \(4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) catches and sticks to a body of mass \(1\,\text{kg}\) initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. Immediately after sticking, the velocity of the centre of mass of the combined system is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(m_1=3\,\text{kg}\), \(v_1=4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(m_2=1\,\text{kg}\), and \(v_2=0\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Centre-of-mass velocity of the combined system.
\( \textbf{Use total momentum:} \)
\[
P=m_1v_1+m_2v_2
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
P=(3)(4)+(1)(0)
\]
\[
P=12\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Total mass:} \)
\[
M=3\,\text{kg}+1\,\text{kg}=4\,\text{kg}
\]
\( \textbf{Relation with centre-of-mass velocity:} \)
\[
P=MV_{\text{CM}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
V_{\text{CM}}=\frac{P}{M}=\frac{12}{4}\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\[
V_{\text{CM}}=3\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass of the combined system moves at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) in the original direction of the \(3\,\text{kg}\) body.

question: Newton's second law for a system of particles is most generally written as
explanation: For a system of particles, Newton's second law connects the net external force with the rate of change of total momentum. The total momentum is \(\vec{P}=\sum \vec{p}_i\), so the law is written as \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}\). Internal forces between particles of the system cancel in pairs in the total force balance. If the total mass is constant, this relation can also be written as \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=M\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\). The word external is essential because internal interactions can change individual motions without changing the system's total momentum through their own pairwise action.

question: A system has constant total mass \(M\). If its centre of mass has acceleration \(\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\), the net external force on the system is
explanation: For a constant-mass system, total momentum is \(\vec{P}=M\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\). Differentiating with respect to time gives \(\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}=M\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\). Newton's second law for a system says that \(\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}\) equals the net external force. Therefore, \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=M\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\). This relation describes the acceleration of the centre of mass, not necessarily the acceleration of every particle inside the system.

question: Two particles inside a system exert equal and opposite forces on each other along the same line. In the equation for the whole system, these two forces
opt_a: add to give the net external force
opt_b: cancel from the internal force sum
opt_c: double the acceleration of the centre of mass
opt_d: become the total momentum of the system
explanation: Internal forces occur between particles that both belong to the chosen system. For ordinary pair interactions, the force of particle P on particle Q and the force of particle Q on particle P are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. When forces are summed for the whole system, such an action-reaction pair contributes zero resultant. This cancellation is why the motion of the centre of mass is controlled by net external force. The internal forces can still affect relative motion, so cancellation in the system equation does not mean the forces are absent.

question: A \(6\,\text{kg}\) system has momentum changing from \(12\,\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) to \(30\,\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) in \(3\,\text{s}\). The average external force on the system is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial momentum:} \) \(\vec{P}_i=12\,\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Final momentum:} \) \(\vec{P}_f=30\,\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Time interval:} \) \(\Delta t=3\,\text{s}\).
\( \textbf{Average force relation:} \)
\[
\vec{F}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{\Delta \vec{P}}{\Delta t}
\]
\( \textbf{Momentum change:} \)
\[
\Delta \vec{P}=\vec{P}_f-\vec{P}_i
\]
\[
\Delta \vec{P}=30\,\hat{i}-12\,\hat{i}=18\,\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\vec{F}_{\text{avg}}=\frac{18\,\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}}{3\,\text{s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\vec{F}_{\text{avg}}=6\,\hat{i}\,\text{N}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The average external force is \(6\,\hat{i}\,\text{N}\).

question:
Study the table and identify the row that follows Newton's second law for a system.
RowSystem conditionSystem-level result
P\(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}\ne 0\)\(\vec{P}\) may change with time
QOnly internal forces act\(\vec{P}\) must change because particles interact
R\(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=0\)\(\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\) must be infinite
SMasses are unequal\(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}\) cannot be defined
explanation: Row P agrees with \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}\), because a non-zero net external force can change total momentum. Row Q is wrong because internal forces alone do not change the total momentum of the whole system when they cancel in pairs. Row R is wrong because \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=0\) gives \(\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}=0\) for a constant-mass system, not an infinite acceleration. Row S is also wrong because unequal masses are handled normally in system mechanics. The system law depends on the net external force, not on the masses being equal.

question:
Assertion: The acceleration of the centre of mass of a system is decided by the net external force on the system.
Reason: Internal forces between particles of the system cancel in the total force balance.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The assertion is true because a system with constant total mass obeys \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=M\vec{A}_{\text{CM}}\). This equation shows that the centre-of-mass acceleration is controlled by the net external force. The reason is also true because internal forces occur in equal and opposite pairs for particles inside the system. Their cancellation removes them from the net force equation of the whole system. The reason explains why the external force, rather than the internal force sum, appears in the centre-of-mass equation.

question: A \(4\,\text{kg}\) cart contains a \(1\,\text{kg}\) block. A horizontal force of \(10\,\text{N}\) acts on the cart-block system as a whole, and friction with the ground is negligible. The acceleration of the centre of mass of the cart-block system is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Chosen system:} \) Cart plus block.
\( \textbf{Masses:} \) Cart mass \(=4\,\text{kg}\), block mass \(=1\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Total mass:} \)
\[
M=4\,\text{kg}+1\,\text{kg}=5\,\text{kg}
\]
\( \textbf{External force:} \) \(F_{\text{ext}}=10\,\text{N}\).
\( \textbf{System equation:} \)
\[
F_{\text{ext}}=MA_{\text{CM}}
\]
\( \textbf{Rearrange:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{F_{\text{ext}}}{M}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=\frac{10\,\text{N}}{5\,\text{kg}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
A_{\text{CM}}=2\,\text{m s}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{System-choice note:} \) Forces between cart and block are internal for this chosen system.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The centre of mass accelerates at \(2\,\text{m s}^{-2}\).

question: Use the arrangement described below. Two blocks are connected by a light string and pulled on a smooth table. If both blocks together are chosen as the system, the tension in the string is
opt_a: an internal force that cancels for the chosen system
opt_b: an external force that acts on the two-block system
opt_c: the only external force on the two-block system
opt_d: a quantity equal to the total momentum of the system
explanation: When both blocks are included in the chosen system, the string force on one block and the string force on the other block are internal forces. These two tension forces act in opposite directions on different blocks. In the force equation for the whole two-block system, their contributions cancel. The acceleration of the centre of mass is then decided by the external pull and any other external forces. If only one block were chosen as the system, the same tension would be an external force on that smaller system.

question: A graph of total momentum \(P_x\) of a system versus time \(t\) is a straight line with slope \(-5\,\text{N}\). The net external force along the \(x\)-direction is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Graph quantity:} \) The vertical axis is total momentum component \(P_x\).
\( \textbf{Horizontal axis:} \) The horizontal axis is time \(t\).
\( \textbf{Slope meaning:} \)
\[
\text{slope}=\frac{dP_x}{dt}
\]
\( \textbf{System law:} \)
\[
F_{\text{ext},x}=\frac{dP_x}{dt}
\]
\( \textbf{Given slope:} \)
\[
\frac{dP_x}{dt}=-5\,\text{N}
\]
\( \textbf{Therefore:} \)
\[
F_{\text{ext},x}=-5\,\text{N}
\]
\( \textbf{Sign meaning:} \) The negative sign shows that the net external force is along the negative \(x\)-direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The net external force along the \(x\)-direction is \(-5\,\text{N}\).

question: A shell moving horizontally explodes into fragments in mid-air. During the short explosion, gravity is the only significant external force. For the horizontal motion of the fragments considered as one system,
opt_a: each fragment must have the same horizontal velocity
opt_c: horizontal total momentum becomes zero instantly
explanation: During the explosion, the forces between fragments are internal forces. Gravity acts vertically, so it has no horizontal component. Therefore, the net external force in the horizontal direction is approximately zero during the short explosion. From \(F_{\text{ext},x}=\frac{dP_x}{dt}\), zero horizontal external force means \(P_x\) remains constant. The fragments can have different horizontal velocities, but their vector momentum sum in the horizontal direction remains the same.

question: Linear momentum of a system is conserved when
opt_a: the net external force on the system is zero
opt_d: all particles are at rest relative to one another
explanation: Conservation of linear momentum follows from \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}\). If \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=0\), then \(\frac{d\vec{P}}{dt}=0\), so the total momentum \(\vec{P}\) remains constant. Internal forces may be present and may even be very large, as in explosions or collisions. Equal masses are not required for momentum conservation. The condition concerns the net external force on the chosen system, not the details of internal motion.

question: Two carts on a smooth horizontal track are initially at rest with a compressed spring between them. After release, the \(2\,\text{kg}\) cart moves left with speed \(3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The speed of the \(3\,\text{kg}\) cart is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial momentum:} \) The system is initially at rest, so total momentum is \(0\).
\( \textbf{Choose direction:} \) Take right as positive.
\( \textbf{Known velocity:} \) The \(2\,\text{kg}\) cart moves left, so \(v_1=-3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Unknown velocity:} \) Let the \(3\,\text{kg}\) cart have velocity \(v_2\).
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[
m_1v_1+m_2v_2=0
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
(2)(-3)+(3)v_2=0
\]
\( \textbf{Simplify:} \)
\[
-6+3v_2=0
\]
\[
3v_2=6
\]
\( \textbf{Solve:} \)
\[
v_2=2\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction:} \) The positive sign means the \(3\,\text{kg}\) cart moves to the right.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The \(3\,\text{kg}\) cart moves with speed \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) to the right.

question:
Consider the following statements about conservation of linear momentum.
I. It applies to a chosen system when the net external force is zero.
II. It can apply even when strong internal forces act.
III. It requires the centre of mass to be at rest in every inertial frame.
explanation: Statement I is true because zero net external force gives constant total momentum. Statement II is also true because internal forces cancel in the total momentum equation for the whole system. Statement III is false because a conserved total momentum can be non-zero, in which case the centre of mass moves with constant non-zero velocity. Conservation does not mean rest; it means no change with time. A system can move uniformly as a whole while still conserving momentum.

question:
Read the case below and answer the question.
A person standing on a smooth cart throws a heavy bag forward. The cart and person start moving backward after the throw. Treat the person, cart, and bag as one system during the throw, and neglect horizontal external force.
Why does the cart-person part move backward?
opt_a: the centre of mass accelerates forward
opt_c: internal forces fail to act during the throw
opt_d: the thrown bag loses all its momentum
explanation: The force between the person and the bag is internal when the person, cart, and bag are chosen as one system. With negligible horizontal external force, the total horizontal momentum of the system remains constant. If the system was initially at rest, the forward momentum of the thrown bag must be balanced by backward momentum of the cart-person part. This does not mean the bag has no momentum; it means the momenta add vectorially to the original total. The backward motion is a direct result of momentum conservation for the whole system.

question: A \(60\,\text{kg}\) person jumps from a stationary \(20\,\text{kg}\) boat onto a pier with horizontal speed \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) relative to the water. Neglect horizontal external force during the jump. The recoil speed of the boat is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial state:} \) Person and boat are initially at rest, so total horizontal momentum is \(0\).
\( \textbf{Choose direction:} \) Take the person's jump direction as positive.
\( \textbf{Person momentum after jump:} \)
\[
p_{\text{person}}=(60)(2)=120\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Boat velocity:} \) Let the boat velocity be \(v_b\).
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[
p_{\text{person}}+p_{\text{boat}}=0
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
120+(20)v_b=0
\]
\( \textbf{Solve for boat velocity:} \)
\[
20v_b=-120
\]
\[
v_b=-6\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Speed:} \) The recoil speed is the magnitude, \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The boat recoils with speed \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) opposite to the person's jump.

question: A collision between two balls occurs on a smooth horizontal table. During the short collision, the force between the balls is much larger than friction. The most suitable reason for treating horizontal momentum as conserved is that
opt_a: collision forces cancel for the two-ball system
opt_b: each ball has zero horizontal momentum during contact
opt_c: the balls must have exactly equal masses
opt_d: the centre of mass stops at the instant of collision
explanation: During a short collision, the force of one ball on the other and the force of the other ball on the first are internal forces for the two-ball system. These forces are large, but they are equal and opposite in the total force balance. If horizontal external forces are negligible during the short time interval, the total horizontal momentum is conserved. The individual momenta of the balls can change greatly. Momentum conservation is a system statement, not a claim that either ball has zero momentum during contact.

question: A system has constant total momentum \(\vec{P}\). Its centre of mass must
opt_a: remain permanently at rest at the origin
opt_b: move automatically in a circular path
explanation: The total momentum of a system is related to centre-of-mass velocity by \(\vec{P}=M\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\). If \(M\) is constant and \(\vec{P}\) is constant, then \(\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\) is also constant. The centre of mass may be at rest only if \(\vec{P}=0\). If \(\vec{P}\ne 0\), it moves uniformly in the direction of \(\vec{P}\). Constant momentum means uniform centre-of-mass motion, not necessarily zero motion.

question: A \(5\,\text{kg}\) object moving at \(6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) breaks into two parts of masses \(2\,\text{kg}\) and \(3\,\text{kg}\). The \(2\,\text{kg}\) part continues forward at \(9\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The speed of the \(3\,\text{kg}\) part is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial momentum:} \)
\[
P_i=(5)(6)=30\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{After breaking:} \) The \(2\,\text{kg}\) part has speed \(9\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) forward.
\( \textbf{Momentum of the lighter part:} \)
\[
p_1=(2)(9)=18\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Define the heavier part speed:} \)
\[
p_2=3v
\]
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[
P_i=p_1+p_2
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
30=18+3v
\]
\( \textbf{Solve:} \)
\[
3v=12
\]
\[
v=4\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction check:} \) The result is positive, so the \(3\,\text{kg}\) part also moves forward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The \(3\,\text{kg}\) part moves at \(4\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: If an isolated system has total momentum \(\vec{P}\ne \vec{0}\), its centre of mass
opt_b: accelerates in the direction of internal forces
opt_c: must remain fixed at one point
explanation: For a system of constant mass, total momentum is related to centre-of-mass velocity by \(\vec{P}=M\vec{V}_{\text{CM}}\). If the system is isolated, the net external force is zero, so \(\vec{P}\) remains constant. When \(\vec{P}\ne \vec{0}\), the centre-of-mass velocity is also non-zero and constant. Internal collisions or explosions can change the velocities of the individual particles, but they do not change the uniform motion of the centre of mass. Rest of the centre of mass is only the special case \(\vec{P}=\vec{0}\).

question: A \(2\,\text{kg}\) body moving east at \(5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) collides and sticks to a \(3\,\text{kg}\) body moving east at \(1\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). On a smooth horizontal surface, their common velocity after sticking is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(m_1=2\,\text{kg}\), \(v_1=5\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(m_2=3\,\text{kg}\), and \(v_2=1\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{System condition:} \) The horizontal surface is smooth, so horizontal external force is negligible during the collision.
\( \textbf{Initial total momentum:} \)
\[
P_i=m_1v_1+m_2v_2
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
P_i=(2)(5)+(3)(1)
\]
\[
P_i=10+3=13\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Combined mass after sticking:} \)
\[
M=2\,\text{kg}+3\,\text{kg}=5\,\text{kg}
\]
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[
P_i=Mv
\]
\( \textbf{Final velocity:} \)
\[
v=\frac{13}{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}=2.6\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction:} \) The positive result means motion remains eastward.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The common velocity is \(2.6\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) east.

question:
Use the graph description below.
For a chosen system, a graph of total momentum component \(P_x\) versus time \(t\) is a horizontal straight line above the time axis.
The graph indicates that
opt_a: the centre of mass is necessarily at rest
opt_b: all internal forces are absent from the system
opt_c: \(P_x\) is constant because net external force along \(x\) is zero
opt_d: net external force along \(x\) is positive and increasing uniformly
explanation: The slope of a \(P_x\)-versus-\(t\) graph gives \(\frac{dP_x}{dt}\). For a system of particles, \(\frac{dP_x}{dt}=F_{\text{ext},x}\). A horizontal line has zero slope, so the net external force component along \(x\) is zero. The line being above the time axis means \(P_x\) is constant but non-zero. A constant non-zero momentum corresponds to uniform centre-of-mass motion along \(x\), not necessarily rest.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that misuses conservation of linear momentum.
RowSituationConclusion
PTwo carts push apart on a smooth trackTotal horizontal momentum remains constant
QFragments of a shell during a very short explosionInternal forces may change individual momenta
RA ball falling freely under gravityVertical momentum of the ball alone is conserved
STwo balls collide on a smooth tableTotal horizontal momentum is approximately conserved
explanation: Row R is the unsuitable conclusion because a freely falling ball has an external gravitational force acting on it. Its vertical momentum changes with time due to this external force. Rows P and S are valid horizontal momentum examples when external horizontal force is negligible. Row Q is also valid because internal forces can strongly change the momenta of individual fragments while the system momentum follows the external-force condition. Momentum conservation is applied component by component according to the external force in that direction.

question: A body initially at rest breaks into three fragments on a smooth horizontal surface. Two fragments have momenta \(6\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\) and \(8\hat{j}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\). The momentum of the third fragment is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Initial condition:} \) The body is initially at rest, so the initial total momentum is \(\vec{0}\).
\( \textbf{External-force condition:} \) The surface is smooth, so horizontal external force is negligible.
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[
\vec{p}_1+\vec{p}_2+\vec{p}_3=\vec{0}
\]
\( \textbf{Known fragment momenta:} \)
\[
\vec{p}_1=6\hat{i}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\[
\vec{p}_2=8\hat{j}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Solve for third momentum:} \)
\[
\vec{p}_3=-(\vec{p}_1+\vec{p}_2)
\]
\[
\vec{p}_3=-(6\hat{i}+8\hat{j})\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final vector:} \)
\[
\vec{p}_3=-6\hat{i}-8\hat{j}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Vector check:} \) The three momentum vectors must add to zero, not merely have equal magnitudes.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The third fragment has momentum \(-6\hat{i}-8\hat{j}\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}\).

question:
Consider the following statements about recoil and explosion examples.
I. They are commonly analysed by choosing a system that includes all separating parts.
II. Momentum conservation can hold even though kinetic energy may change.
III. Momentum conservation requires every fragment to move with equal speed.
explanation: Statement I is true because recoil and explosion problems are system problems; all interacting parts must be included for internal forces to cancel. Statement II is true because momentum conservation depends on net external force, while kinetic energy can change due to internal energy release or deformation. Statement III is false because different fragments can have different masses, directions, and speeds. Their vector momenta must combine according to conservation, not their speeds alone. The reliable conserved quantity under zero net external force is total momentum.

question: A \(4\,\text{kg}\) object moving at \(3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) breaks into two parts. One part of mass \(1\,\text{kg}\) moves backward at \(2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The speed of the other part is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Choose direction:} \) Take the original direction of motion as positive.
\( \textbf{Initial momentum:} \)
\[
P_i=(4)(3)=12\,\text{kg m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Masses after breaking:} \) One part has mass \(1\,\text{kg}\), so the other part has mass \(3\,\text{kg}\).
\( \textbf{Known velocity after breaking:} \) The \(1\,\text{kg}\) part moves backward, so \(v_1=-2\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Define the heavier part velocity:} \)
\[
P_f=(1)(-2)+(3)v
\]
\( \textbf{Momentum conservation:} \)
\[
P_i=P_f
\]
\[
12=-2+3v
\]
\( \textbf{Solve:} \)
\[
3v=14
\]
\[
v=\frac{14}{3}\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Direction check:} \) The positive sign means the heavier remaining part moves in the original direction.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The other part moves with speed \(\frac{14}{3}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

question: A system is said to be isolated in the linear-momentum sense when
opt_a: internal forces are absent between its particles
opt_b: net external force on the chosen system is zero
opt_c: every particle inside the system is at rest
opt_d: its centre of mass is located at the origin
explanation: For conservation of linear momentum, the important condition is \(\vec{F}_{\text{ext}}=0\). Internal forces may still act, and they may be responsible for collisions, recoil, or explosions inside the system. The system does not have to be at rest; it can have constant non-zero total momentum. The centre of mass also need not be at the origin, because origin choice is only a coordinate convention. Isolation for momentum conservation is about the absence of net external force on the chosen system.

question: In a variable-mass situation such as a rocket ejecting fuel, the ordinary centre-of-mass formula should be applied carefully because
opt_a: centre of mass has no meaning for moving bodies
opt_b: ejected mass may leave the chosen system
opt_c: mass can never leave a mechanical system
opt_d: internal forces stop obeying Newton's third law
explanation: Centre-of-mass and momentum formulas apply to a clearly chosen system. In a rocket-like situation, fuel may be ejected and may or may not be included in the chosen system. If the system is taken as the rocket alone after fuel leaves, its mass is changing and the simple constant-mass relation must not be used carelessly. If the rocket plus ejected fuel is chosen, the system description is different. The caution is about system choice, not about centre of mass becoming meaningless.

question: A rocket and its fuel are initially treated as one system. After some fuel is expelled, a calculation that considers only the remaining rocket must
opt_a: assume the centre of mass is always at the rocket's nose
opt_b: keep using the original total mass without question
opt_c: specify that the chosen system has changed
opt_d: ignore the velocity of the expelled fuel in every case
explanation: The original system includes the rocket and all its fuel. After fuel is expelled, considering only the remaining rocket excludes matter that was previously part of the system. This means the system boundary has changed. Momentum and centre-of-mass statements depend on what is included inside the boundary. Without a clear system choice, it is easy to mix the motion of the rocket alone with the motion of the rocket-plus-fuel system.

question: A leaking cart moves on a smooth horizontal track while sand falls vertically out of it. If the chosen system is "cart plus the sand that has not yet fallen out," the system mass
opt_d: equals only the mass of fallen sand
explanation: The chosen system includes the cart and only the sand still inside it. As sand leaves the cart, that sand is no longer part of the chosen system. Therefore, the mass of the chosen system decreases with time. This is a variable-mass description and must be handled with care. If instead the system included the cart, remaining sand, and fallen sand together, the total mass description would be different.

question: A statement says, "Whenever mass leaves a body, linear momentum conservation cannot be used at all." The best evaluation is that the statement is
opt_a: true because changing mass destroys momentum conservation
opt_b: false because external forces are never present
opt_c: false if a larger system has zero net external force
opt_d: true because centre of mass is undefined
explanation: Momentum conservation is not rejected merely because mass leaves one part of a system. The key is to choose the system properly and check the net external force. For example, the rocket plus expelled gases may be treated together over a short interval if external effects are negligible. Momentum can then be conserved for that larger system, even though the rocket alone has changing mass. The unsafe step is applying a constant-mass formula to a changing subsystem without redefining the system.

question:
Match the situation with the suitable system-choice caution.
Column IColumn II
P. Explosion into fragments1. Include all fragments for total momentum conservation
Q. Rocket ejecting fuel2. Decide whether ejected fuel is part of the system
R. Two carts pushing apart3. Spring forces are internal if both carts are included
S. Single cart chosen alone4. Contact or string force from outside may be external
explanation: In an explosion, all fragments should be included when applying total momentum conservation. In a rocket-like case, the system choice must state whether the ejected fuel is included. For two carts pushing apart, the spring forces are internal if both carts are chosen together. If only one cart is chosen, a force from the other cart, string, or spring may be external. The same physical force can change classification when the system boundary changes.

question: A variable-mass caution is most closely connected with the idea that
opt_a: the set of masses in the system must be chosen clearly
opt_b: centre of mass can be used only when all masses form a rigid body
opt_c: momentum is conserved only for equal masses
opt_d: all ejected material must be ignored
explanation: Centre-of-mass formulas are always applied to a definite system. The masses \(m_i\), positions \(\vec{r}_i\), and total mass \(M\) must refer to the same chosen set of matter. In variable-mass situations, matter may enter or leave the object being watched, so the system boundary needs extra care. The centre of mass can still be defined, but the calculation must match the system being described. The main caution is consistency of system choice, not rejection of centre-of-mass ideas.

question: The vector product \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) gives a quantity whose direction is
opt_a: along \(\vec{A}\) in the plane of the two vectors
opt_b: along \(\vec{B}\) in the plane of the two vectors
opt_c: perpendicular to the plane of \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\)
opt_d: opposite to \(\vec{A}+\vec{B}\) in the same plane
explanation: The cross product of two vectors is itself a vector. Its magnitude depends on the magnitudes of the two vectors and the sine of the angle between them. Its direction is not along either original vector in general. Instead, \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to the plane containing \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\). The choice between the two perpendicular directions is made by the right-hand rule.

question: The magnitude of the vector product \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) is
explanation: If the angle between \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\) is \(\theta\), the magnitude of their cross product is \(AB\sin\theta\). This formula uses the component of one vector perpendicular to the other. The factor \(\sin\theta\) makes the product zero when the vectors are parallel and maximum when they are perpendicular. The expression \(AB\cos\theta\) belongs to the scalar product, not the vector product. Remembering the perpendicular-component idea helps separate cross product from dot product.

question: Two non-zero vectors are parallel to each other. The magnitude of their cross product is
explanation: For parallel vectors, the angle between them is either \(0^\circ\) or \(180^\circ\). The magnitude of the cross product is \(AB\sin\theta\). Since \(\sin 0^\circ=0\) and \(\sin 180^\circ=0\), the cross product has zero magnitude. This does not mean either vector is zero; it means there is no perpendicular component of one vector relative to the other. A cross product measures perpendicularity, so parallel vectors give no vector product.

question: The magnitude of \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) is maximum when the angle between \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\) is
explanation: The cross product magnitude is \(AB\sin\theta\). For fixed \(A\) and \(B\), only \(\sin\theta\) controls how the magnitude changes with angle. The maximum value of \(\sin\theta\) is \(1\), which occurs at \(\theta=90^\circ\). Hence the maximum cross product magnitude is \(AB\). This is why a force applied perpendicular to a position vector gives the largest torque for the same \(r\) and \(F\).

question: If \(A=3\) units, \(B=4\) units, and the angle between \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\) is \(30^\circ\), then \(|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(A=3\), \(B=4\), and \(\theta=30^\circ\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Magnitude of the cross product \(|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|\).
\( \textbf{Formula:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=AB\sin\theta
\]
\( \textbf{Why this applies:} \) The question gives two vector magnitudes and the angle between them.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=(3)(4)\sin30^\circ
\]
\( \textbf{Use the sine value:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=12\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=6
\]
\( \textbf{Unit idea:} \) The unit is the product of the units of \(A\) and \(B\); for two lengths, it would be square units.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The magnitude is \(6\) square units.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that correctly describes \(|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|\) for fixed non-zero \(A\) and \(B\).
RowAngle \(\theta\)\(|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|\)
P\(0^\circ\)\(AB\)
Q\(90^\circ\)\(AB\)
R\(180^\circ\)\(AB\)
S\(30^\circ\)\(0\)
explanation: The cross product magnitude is \(AB\sin\theta\). At \(\theta=0^\circ\), \(\sin0^\circ=0\), so row P is not suitable. At \(\theta=90^\circ\), \(\sin90^\circ=1\), so the magnitude is \(AB\), making row Q suitable. At \(\theta=180^\circ\), the magnitude is again zero, not \(AB\). At \(\theta=30^\circ\), the magnitude is \(\frac{AB}{2}\), not zero.

question: The order of vectors in a cross product matters because
explanation: Cross product is anti-commutative. Reversing the order of the vectors does not change the magnitude, because \(AB\sin\theta\) remains the same. However, the direction reverses because the right-hand rule gives the opposite perpendicular direction. Therefore, \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) and \(\vec{B}\times\vec{A}\) are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction. This order sensitivity is important in torque \(\vec{\tau}=\vec{r}\times\vec{F}\) and angular momentum \(\vec{L}=\vec{r}\times\vec{p}\).

question:
Assertion: If \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\) are perpendicular, then \(|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=AB\).
Reason: For perpendicular vectors, \(\sin\theta=1\).
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The assertion is true because the cross product magnitude is \(AB\sin\theta\). When two vectors are perpendicular, \(\theta=90^\circ\). Since \(\sin90^\circ=1\), the magnitude becomes \(AB\). The reason gives the exact mathematical step that makes the assertion true. The result is not because the vectors are equal in magnitude; it is because their angle makes the sine factor maximum.

question: Geometrically, the magnitude of \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) represents the area of
opt_b: a rectangle with sides \(A\) and \(B\) at all angles
opt_d: a triangle formed by \(\vec{A}\), \(\vec{B}\), and the resultant
explanation: The area of a parallelogram formed by two adjacent vectors is base times height. If \(A\) is taken as the base, the perpendicular height contributed by \(\vec{B}\) is \(B\sin\theta\). Therefore, the area is \(A(B\sin\theta)=AB\sin\theta\). This is exactly \(|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|\). The area interpretation also explains why the cross product becomes zero when the two vectors are parallel.

question:
Use the graph description below.
For fixed non-zero vectors with magnitudes \(A\) and \(B\), a graph is plotted between \(|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|\) and the angle \(\theta\) from \(0^\circ\) to \(180^\circ\).
The graph has
opt_a: the same non-zero value for every angle
explanation:
\( \textbf{Relation:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=AB\sin\theta
\]
\( \textbf{Fixed quantities:} \) \(A\) and \(B\) are constant, so the angle dependence comes from \(\sin\theta\).
\( \textbf{At zero degrees:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=AB\sin0^\circ=0
\]
\( \textbf{At ninety degrees:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=AB\sin90^\circ=AB
\]
\( \textbf{At one hundred eighty degrees:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=AB\sin180^\circ=0
\]
\( \textbf{Graph meaning:} \) The curve rises from zero to a maximum and then falls back to zero.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The graph is zero at \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\), with maximum at \(90^\circ\).

question: If \(\vec{A}\) is doubled, \(\vec{B}\) is tripled, and the angle between them remains unchanged, then \(|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|\) becomes
explanation:
\( \textbf{Original magnitude:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|=AB\sin\theta
\]
\( \textbf{New magnitudes:} \) \(A'=2A\) and \(B'=3B\).
\( \textbf{Angle condition:} \) The angle remains \(\theta\), so the sine factor is unchanged.
\( \textbf{New cross product magnitude:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}'\times\vec{B}'|=(2A)(3B)\sin\theta
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}'\times\vec{B}'|=6AB\sin\theta
\]
\( \textbf{Comparison:} \)
\[
|\vec{A}'\times\vec{B}'|=6|\vec{A}\times\vec{B}|
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The magnitude becomes \(6\) times the original value.

question: Take east as \(+\hat{i}\), north as \(+\hat{j}\), and upward as \(+\hat{k}\). The direction of \(\hat{i}\times\hat{j}\) is
explanation: In the standard right-handed coordinate system, \(\hat{i}\), \(\hat{j}\), and \(\hat{k}\) point along the positive \(x\)-, \(y\)-, and \(z\)-directions. The basic unit-vector cross product is \(\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}\). With east as \(+\hat{i}\) and north as \(+\hat{j}\), \(\hat{k}\) corresponds to upward. The order matters because \(\hat{j}\times\hat{i}=-\hat{k}\). This is an early direction convention needed before using torque and angular momentum directions.

question: Use the arrangement described below. A vector \(\vec{A}\) points along \(+\hat{i}\), and a vector \(\vec{B}\) points along \(-\hat{j}\). The direction of \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) is
explanation: The direction of \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) follows the right-hand rule and the unit-vector products. Here, \(\vec{A}\) is along \(+\hat{i}\), while \(\vec{B}\) is along \(-\hat{j}\). Therefore, the direction is \(\hat{i}\times(-\hat{j})=-(\hat{i}\times\hat{j})\). Since \(\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}\), the result is \(-\hat{k}\). The negative sign comes from the direction of \(\vec{B}\), not from any change in magnitude.

question:
Match the vector-pair condition with the cross-product result.
Column IColumn II
P. Vectors parallel1. Cross product magnitude is \(0\)
Q. Vectors perpendicular2. Cross product magnitude is \(AB\)
R. Order reversed3. Direction reverses
S. Same vector crossed with itself4. Cross product is \(\vec{0}\)
explanation: Parallel vectors have \(\theta=0^\circ\) or \(180^\circ\), so \(AB\sin\theta=0\). Perpendicular vectors have \(\theta=90^\circ\), so the magnitude becomes \(AB\). Reversing the order changes \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) into \(\vec{B}\times\vec{A}\), which has the opposite direction. A vector crossed with itself has zero angle with itself, so the result is \(\vec{0}\). These matches combine the magnitude and direction properties of cross product.

question: A student writes \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=\vec{B}\times\vec{A}\) because both have magnitude \(AB\sin\theta\). The best correction is that
opt_c: both products are always zero vectors
opt_d: same magnitude and same direction always
explanation: The magnitude of \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) and \(\vec{B}\times\vec{A}\) is the same because the angle between the two vectors is the same. However, cross product is a vector, so direction must also be considered. The right-hand rule gives opposite perpendicular directions when the order of the vectors is reversed. Thus, \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}=-(\vec{B}\times\vec{A})\). Equality of magnitude alone is not enough to make two vectors equal.

question: Two vectors have magnitudes \(5\,\text{N}\) and \(2\,\text{m}\), and the angle between them is \(90^\circ\). If they are used in the order \(\vec{r}\times\vec{F}\), the magnitude of the result is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(r=2\,\text{m}\), \(F=5\,\text{N}\), and \(\theta=90^\circ\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Magnitude of \(\vec{r}\times\vec{F}\).
\( \textbf{Cross product magnitude:} \)
\[
|\vec{r}\times\vec{F}|=rF\sin\theta
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
|\vec{r}\times\vec{F}|=(2)(5)\sin90^\circ
\]
\( \textbf{Use the perpendicular-angle sine value:} \)
\[
|\vec{r}\times\vec{F}|=10
\]
\( \textbf{Unit product:} \)
\[
\text{m}\cdot\text{N}=\text{N m}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation result:} \)
\[
|\vec{r}\times\vec{F}|=10\,\text{N m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The magnitude is \(10\,\text{N m}\).

question: In the expression \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\), if \(\vec{B}\) is resolved into a component parallel to \(\vec{A}\) and a component perpendicular to \(\vec{A}\), only the perpendicular component contributes because
opt_a: the parallel component is always larger
opt_c: the perpendicular component has zero magnitude
explanation: The cross product magnitude depends on the perpendicular part of one vector relative to the other. The component of \(\vec{B}\) parallel to \(\vec{A}\) makes an angle \(0^\circ\) or \(180^\circ\) with \(\vec{A}\). Such a component gives zero cross product because the sine factor is zero. The perpendicular component gives the full effective contribution because its angle with \(\vec{A}\) is \(90^\circ\). This is why \(AB\sin\theta\) can be read as \(A\) multiplied by the perpendicular component of \(B\).

question: A vector product is chosen instead of a scalar product when the required physical quantity must
opt_a: remain unchanged after reversing the order
opt_b: be a vector perpendicular to the vector plane
opt_c: be a scalar number with no directional character
opt_d: always point along the first vector
explanation: A scalar product gives a scalar quantity, while a vector product gives a vector quantity. The direction of a cross product is perpendicular to the plane of the two vectors involved. This is why cross product is used in quantities such as torque and angular momentum, where an axial direction is needed. The order of vectors cannot be ignored because reversing the order reverses the direction. The vector product is selected when both perpendicular magnitude and perpendicular direction carry physical meaning.

question: In applying the right-hand rule for \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\), the fingers of the right hand are curled from
opt_a: the thumb toward the palm, and the fingers give \(AB\sin\theta\)
explanation: The order of vectors is essential in a cross product. For \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\), the right-hand fingers are curled from the direction of \(\vec{A}\) toward the direction of \(\vec{B}\) through the smaller angle. The extended thumb then gives the direction of the product. If the curling order is reversed, the thumb points in the opposite direction. This is why \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) and \(\vec{B}\times\vec{A}\) have opposite directions even when their magnitudes are equal.

question: Take \(+\hat{i}\) as east, \(+\hat{j}\) as north, and \(+\hat{k}\) as upward. A vector \(\vec{A}\) points north and a vector \(\vec{B}\) points east. The direction of \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) is
explanation: North is represented by \(+\hat{j}\), and east is represented by \(+\hat{i}\). The required product is therefore \(\hat{j}\times\hat{i}\). Since \(\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}\), reversing the order gives \(\hat{j}\times\hat{i}=-\hat{k}\). The direction \(-\hat{k}\) is downward. The result differs from the east-cross-north case because the order of the two vectors has been reversed.

question: A vector \(\vec{A}\) lies in the plane of a page toward the right, and \(\vec{B}\) lies in the same plane upward. The direction of \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) is
explanation: Let right be \(+\hat{i}\) and upward in the page be \(+\hat{j}\). The cross product is then \(\hat{i}\times\hat{j}\), which equals \(+\hat{k}\). In the usual right-handed page convention, \(+\hat{k}\) points out of the page. The product is not along either vector because a cross product is perpendicular to the plane containing the two vectors. Reversing the order to \(\vec{B}\times\vec{A}\) would point into the page.

question: Use the arrangement described below. A vector \(\vec{P}\) points out of the page, and a vector \(\vec{Q}\) points toward the right in the page. Taking right as \(+\hat{i}\), upward as \(+\hat{j}\), and out of the page as \(+\hat{k}\), the direction of \(\vec{P}\times\vec{Q}\) is
explanation: The vector \(\vec{P}\) points out of the page, so it is along \(+\hat{k}\). The vector \(\vec{Q}\) points right, so it is along \(+\hat{i}\). The required unit-vector product is \(\hat{k}\times\hat{i}\). In cyclic order, \(\hat{i}\times\hat{j}=\hat{k}\), \(\hat{j}\times\hat{k}=\hat{i}\), and \(\hat{k}\times\hat{i}=\hat{j}\). Hence the direction is \(+\hat{j}\), which is upward in the page.

question: The cross product \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) is reversed in direction when
opt_a: the magnitudes of both vectors are unchanged
opt_c: the angle between them is kept the same
explanation: Cross product direction is fixed by the right-hand rule and depends on the order of the two vectors. Changing \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) to \(\vec{B}\times\vec{A}\) reverses the direction while keeping the magnitude the same. Multiplying both vectors by positive numbers changes only the magnitude, not the direction. Keeping the same angle also does not decide the sign unless the vector order is known. Direction in cross product is therefore an ordered-vector property, not only an angle property.

question:
Assertion: \(\vec{A}\times\vec{B}\) is perpendicular to both \(\vec{A}\) and \(\vec{B}\).
Reason: The direction of a cross product is normal to the plane containing the two vectors.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
